keep: Babbage's engine was for numbers. She wrote that it need not be.
lede: The fight over whether she wrote the first program has outlasted the machine it was written for.
copy: In October 1842 an Italian engineer, Luigi Menabrea, published an account in French of Charles Babbage's unbuilt Analytical Engine, in the Bibliothèque Universelle de Genève. Lovelace translated it. Babbage asked why she had not written an original paper of her own; she said the thought had not occurred to her, and he suggested she add notes. She added seven, lettered A to G. Babbage remembered them as about three times the length of the memoir. In the text as transcribed they run to some 20,000 words against 8,400 of translation, nearer two and a half. The whole appeared in 1843 in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs. Note G sets out, step by step, how the engine would compute the Bernoulli numbers. That table is what the phrase 'first computer program' points at.

Babbage's own account is the first witness on authorship, and it is more generous than the argument that followed. They discussed the illustrations together and he suggested several, 'but the selection was entirely her own'. So was the algebra, except the Bernoulli numbers, which he offered to work out to save her the trouble. She sent his working back for an amendment, having found a grave mistake in it. She died in 1852, at thirty-six.

Menabrea's memoir is about calculation: the mechanical branch of mathematics, numerical tables, the machine as a better Pascal. In Note A Lovelace wrote that the engine 'might act upon other things besides number', and that if the relations of pitched sounds could be expressed in its notation, 'the engine might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity or extent.' She was describing general-purpose computation a century before there was anything to run it on. She got there by asking not what the machine could calculate, but what calculation is a special case of.

facts.s: Length of Lovelace's Notes A–G against her translation of Menabrea: word count of the Fourmilab transcription of the 1843 Sketch (fourmilab.ch/babbage/sketch.html), counted 6 October 2026; Babbage's own estimate, 'about three times the length of the original memoir', is in Passages from the Life of a Philosopher (1864), chapter 8
Notes appended by Lovelace, lettered A to G: Sketch of the Analytical Engine with notes by the translator (1843), Fourmilab transcription

bio.t: Ada Lovelace: The Making of a Computer Scientist
bio.a: Christopher Hollings, Ursula Martin and Adrian Rice
bio.why: Built on her mathematical papers in the Bodleian, and it engages the case against her instead of restating the legend.

contested: Whether the Bernoulli program is hers, and how much of the Notes. Dorothy Stein's 'Ada: A Life and a Legacy' (1985) is the sceptical life, the one later scholars have had to answer. Babbage's own account cuts both ways: he did the Bernoulli algebra himself, and she corrected it. John Fuegi and Jo Francis, in the IEEE Annals of the History of Computing (2003), read the making of the Notes as hers and credit them with the step from number-crunching to computing in the wider sense. Christopher Hollings, Ursula Martin and Adrian Rice (2018) went back to her mathematical papers in the Bodleian to test Stein's judgement of her ability. A table built by two people writing letters to each other is the kind of authorship the surviving letters can narrow and cannot close.
